Covers who pays under no-fault, including students, Ann Arbor’s crosswalk rule, the roundabouts, the freeways, crashes with University of Michigan vehicles and the six-month Court of Claims notice, TheRide buses, drunk drivers on game days, and the deadlines. Free review. (313) 406-7606.

c.v: At a crosswalk without a working traffic signal, the city’s ordinance (City Code chapter 126, section 10:148) requires a driver to stop for a pedestrian in a crosswalk. It also requires the driver to stop before entering the crosswalk when a pedestrian is standing at the curb or the start of the crosswalk waiting to cross. That goes further than state law. A driver who violated it is evidence of negligence in the pedestrian’s claim. See our

sections.heading: Whose road it is: the City, MDOT, or the University

c.v: Ann Arbor is a city and owns its streets, but four public owners share the roads:

items.v: owns the city streets and sidewalks. A claim for a road, signal, or sidewalk defect requires written notice within 120 days (MCL 691.1402, 691.1402a, 691.1404).
owns I-94, US-23, M-14, and any state trunkline routes through the city. A road-defect claim goes to the Court of Claims, with written notice filed there within 120 days (MCL 691.1404).
owns its campus roads, drives, and parking structures. A claim against it is a claim against the State (see below).

sections.heading: When the other vehicle belongs to the University of Michigan

c.v: The University of Michigan is a constitutional state institution. A crash with a University bus, a University-owned vehicle, or a University police car is a claim against the State, under the motor vehicle exception to governmental immunity (MCL 691.1405). That changes three things:

items.v: The claim is filed in the Michigan Court of Claims and decided by a judge, not a jury.
Written notice, or the claim itself, must be filed within six months of the crash (MCL 600.6431). Missing it can end the claim, even though the ordinary deadline is three years.
A claim against an individual University employee raises separate questions.

sections.heading: Who pays after an Ann Arbor crash

c.v: Your own auto insurer pays these benefits regardless of fault (MCL 500.3107):

items.v: your medical expenses, up to the PIP level you chose
85 percent of lost wages for up to three years, up to the monthly cap DIFS sets each year

c.v: The PIP level is not the same as your liability limits.

Since July 2, 2020, Michigan drivers choose a PIP medical level for each policy: unlimited, $500,000, $250,000, $50,000 for some Medicaid enrollees, or an opt-out for some Medicare enrollees (MCL 500.3107c). That choice is separate from the liability limits that protect the other driver.
Many students do not own a car. A student hit while walking, biking, or riding in someone else’s car claims no-fault benefits in this order (MCL 500.3114, 500.3115, 500.3172):

items.v: a policy in the student’s household, which may be a parent’s policy if the student is still domiciled with the parent

if none applies and the student was riding in a car, the insurer of that car (MCL 500.3114(4)) 3. otherwise, including a student hit while walking or biking, the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan, capped at $250,000 for medical benefits (MCL 500.3115(1))

c.v: Whether a student living in Ann Arbor is still domiciled with a parent depends on the facts.

A crash in Ann Arbor with an out-of-state driver, or involving a student from another state, still follows Michigan’s no-fault rules. Insurers that sell auto insurance in Michigan must provide Michigan benefits for a crash here.

A scooter or e-bike rider hit by a car is generally treated like a pedestrian or cyclist for no-fault purposes, with benefits from the household policy or, if none, the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan. A rider who falls with no car involved generally has no no-fault claim.
A passenger hurt on a TheRide or University bus claims benefits under the bus-passenger priority rules (MCL 500.3114(2)).
The insurer must receive written notice within one year (MCL 500.3145(1)). It must pay each bill within 30 days of reasonable proof, or owe 12 percent interest (MCL 500.3142). See our

A person who owned a car and was required to insure it, but did not, is generally barred from PIP benefits for their own injuries (MCL 500.3113(b)). A driver who was operating their own uninsured vehicle cannot recover pain-and-suffering damages, whoever was at fault (MCL 500.3135(2)(c)).

For pain and suffering, you need a threshold injury: death, serious impairment of body function, or permanent serious disfigurement (MCL 500.3135(1)). A serious impairment is an objectively manifested impairment of an important body function that affects your general ability to lead your normal life. It does not have to be permanent (MCL 500.3135(5);
You can also recover economic losses that no-fault does not cover (MCL 500.3135(3)(c)):

items.v: lost wages beyond the three years or above the monthly cap
medical bills above your chosen PIP level

faqs.question: I was hit in a crosswalk near campus. Who is at fault?

answer.v: Usually the driver. At a crosswalk without a working signal, Ann Arbor’s ordinance requires drivers to stop for pedestrians in a crosswalk and before entering it when a pedestrian is waiting at the curb. A driver who did not stop is evidence of negligence. Your own share of fault, if any, reduces the recovery.

faqs.question: I’m a student and I don’t have a car. Who pays my medical bills?

answer.v: Possibly your parent’s auto policy, if you are still domiciled with your parent. If no household policy applies, you claim through the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan. Your claim for pain and suffering is against the driver.

faqs.question: A University of Michigan bus hit me. Is that different?

answer.v: Yes. The University is part of the State, so the claim goes to the Michigan Court of Claims, and written notice or the claim must be filed within six months of the crash. Your no-fault benefits are paid the usual way.

faqs.question: I was hit at the State and Ellsworth roundabout. Who is at fault?

answer.v: Usually the driver who entered without yielding to traffic already in the circle, or who changed lanes or exited from the wrong lane. The State Police recorded 85 crashes there in 2024, so cameras and witnesses matter.

faqs.question: I was riding a scooter and a car hit me. Does no-fault cover me?

answer.v: Generally yes, through your household policy or, if none, the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan, the same way a cyclist or pedestrian is covered. If you fell with no car involved, no-fault generally does not apply.

faqs.question: How many crashes are there in Ann Arbor?

answer.v: The State Police recorded 2,770 crashes in Ann Arbor in 2024. 5 people were killed, 36 were seriously injured, and 540 were injured in all. 56 crashes involved pedestrians and 68 involved bicyclists.

faqs.question: Is my PIP medical coverage the same as my liability limit?

answer.v: Not necessarily. Your liability limits protect the other driver if you cause a crash. Your PIP medical level is a separate choice on the same policy, and it decides how much of your own medical care no-fault pays.

faqs.question: Where would my Ann Arbor case be filed?

answer.v: Claims up to $25,000 go to the 15th District Court at 301 East Huron Street. Injury suits over $25,000 go to the Washtenaw County Trial Court at 101 East Huron Street. Claims against the University or the State go to the Court of Claims.

- Six months for a claim against the University of Michigan or the State, and 120 days for a road-defect notice against MDOT. - 120 days for a notice to the City. - One year to give your no-fault insurer written notice. - Two years to sue a bar, with a 120-day notice. - Three years to sue the at-fault driver.
